:::{#exm-transpose-not-enough}
#### Why complex vectors use the conjugate transpose

For a real vector $\vx$, $\tp{\vx}\vx = \sumjp x_j^2$ is $0$ only when $\vx$ is the zero vector.
The same formula fails for complex vectors.
Let $\vecf{z} = \tp{(1, i)}$. Then

$$
\ba
\underbrace{\tp{\vecf{z}}}_{1 \times 2}\,\underbrace{\vecf{z}}_{2 \times 1}
&= 1 \cd 1 + i \cd i
&& \text{(multiply entry by entry and add)}
\\
&= 1 + i^2
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 0
&& \text{(} i^2 = -1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

although $\vecf{z} \neq \vzero_{2 \times 1}$.
Using the conjugate transpose instead,

$$
\ba
\underbrace{\vecf{z}^{\mathsf{H}}}_{1 \times 2}\,\underbrace{\vecf{z}}_{2 \times 1}
&= \overline{1} \cd 1 + \overline{i} \cd i
&& \text{(@def-conjugate-transpose)}
\\
&= 1 + (-i) \cd i
&& \text{(conjugate each entry)}
\\
&= 1 - i^2
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= 2
&& \text{(} i^2 = -1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

which is positive, as @thm-zhz-sum-squares guarantees.

:::
